title: QR Code Error Correction: Version, Size and Scan-Failure Checks
description: Scan failures often mean long content, tiny modules or weak contrast, not a low level. Reproduced on the same qrcode 1.5.4 engine as the in-site tool.
content:
When a QR code will not scan, the cause is usually not a correction level that is too low. More often it is the length of the content, the pixels each module receives, the contrast, or the destination the code jumps to. The sections below split the problem into four layers — version, error correction, size and pre-publication verification — and use the QR code generator on this site to reproduce two boundaries: a 384px preview and an over-capacity input.

I. What a QR Code Encodes: Version, Modules and the Data Region

A QR code encodes a run of bytes as a matrix of light and dark modules. DENSO WAVE's version reference gives two rules: versions run from 1 to 40, version 1 is 21×21 modules and version 40 is 177×177 modules, and every step up a version adds 4 modules to each side. A module is one of the light or dark dots that build the symbol — neither a screen pixel nor a physical print size.

Part of the matrix is fixed. Generating https://clovertools.cn at level M with qrcode 1.5.4 and inspecting the matrix shows three 7×7 finder patterns in the corners, plus timing lines of alternating light and dark modules in the row and column at index 6. Swap in different content of the same version and those fixed patterns do not move; data and correction codewords fill only the data region, and the finder and timing patterns themselves carry no payload data. DENSO defines the codeword as the unit of the data region, and one codeword is 8 bits.

So "how big is the QR code" has two answers: the version fixes the module count, the output size fixes the pixels or millimeters per module; mixing them yields lopsided conclusions such as "512 must always be sharper".

II. A Higher Error-Correction Rate Is Not Automatically Safer

The four levels L/M/Q/H are labeled 7%, 15%, 25% and 30% in the tool. DENSO stresses that raising the level strengthens correction while also raising the amount of data the symbol must carry: Q or H suits dirty environments such as factories, L suits clean conditions with a lot of data, and M (15%) is the everyday default.

The percentage is the share of codewords that can be recovered, not a promise that a 30% patch over the symbol still scans. DENSO's example: when 50 of 100 codewords need correcting, 100 Reed-Solomon codewords are required, the total rises to 200, 50 of them can be corrected, and the ratio of 25% corresponds to level Q.

The cost is just as concrete: for the same 329-character link, L chooses version 12 (65×65) while H has to choose version 19 (93×93), and inside a 384px preview the scale per module falls from roughly 5.26 to roughly 3.80. Higher correction means a denser symbol with smaller modules, which can make scanning harder at an unchanged print size. The safer wording is that a higher level tolerates more damage, but the same content comes out denser.

III. Content Length Sets Density: Capacity and Version

The version is decided by the number of content bytes together with the correction level. A binary search in 8-bit byte mode with qrcode 1.5.4 gives single-symbol capacity at version 40 of 2953 bytes for L, 2331 for M, 1663 for Q and 1273 for H; one byte more and the library throws "The amount of data is too big to be stored in a QR Code".

Short content already differs by version. https://clovertools.cn is 22 characters, L and M pick version 2 (25×25), and Q and H pick version 3 (29×29); switch to the 329-character long link and the versions become L 12, M 13, Q 17 and H 19 — 65, 69, 85 and 93 modules per side. Raising correction for the same content pushes the whole symbol up to a denser version.

Over capacity, the tool's behavior is blunt: enter 3000 characters of a at level M and the status bar shows 「生成失败: The amount of data is too big to be stored in a QR Code」 ("generation failed"), the preview keeps showing 「等待生成」 ("waiting to generate") and the download button stays disabled. There is no half-drawn image and no automatic fallback.

Before generating, the tool runs input.value.trim(), so leading and trailing whitespace is dropped while whitespace in the middle is encoded as it stands. To control the content exactly, check in an editor that neither end carries stray characters.

Correction level Recoverable share as labeled in the tool Byte capacity at version 40
L 7% 2953 bytes
M 15% 2331 bytes
Q 25% 1663 bytes
H 30% 1273 bytes

The table holds for 8-bit byte mode only; capacity also changes with the character types in use, so "how much fits" cannot be answered from the level alone.

IV. Size and Pixels per Module: 384px and Print Size

The QR code generator on this site offers 256/384/512, defaults to 384px, fixes margin=4 modules and uses #232019 for the foreground and #ffffff for the background. The quiet zone takes 8 modules in total across both sides and the PNG side length is (modules + 8) × scale; the library sets the scale to width ÷ (modules + 8), so the final side length is exactly the width selected.

What really decides legibility is how many pixels each module gets. At 384px, version 2 (25 modules) has a scale of 384÷33≈11.64, version 3 is 384÷37≈10.38, and version 40 is only 384÷185≈2.08. Rasterizing lands on whole-pixel positions, so neighbouring modules end up with 11 or 12, 10 or 11, and 2 or 3 pixels respectively.

Printing magnifies the gap: 384px at 300dpi is about 32.5mm wide, a version 2 module is about 0.99mm, a version 3 module about 0.88mm, and a version 40 module only about 0.18mm. The last is below 0.2mm, and whether it resolves reliably depends on the printer, the paper and the scanning device — "the preview looks sharp" is not evidence.

Export goes through canvas.toDataURL('image/png'). MDN notes that type defaults to image/png, that the call returns a data URL, and that a canvas which is not origin-clean throws SecurityError. The code here is drawn by a local script, so it can be exported directly.

V. Contrast, Quiet Zone and Color Inversion

Scanners tell modules apart by the light/dark difference. The tool pins the foreground to dark gray #232019 and the background to pure white #ffffff, which by the relative-luminance formula gives a contrast of roughly 16.25:1. The preview footer states 「预览保留白色背景」 ("the preview keeps its white background") and notes that the export includes the quiet zone scanning needs; the exported PNG carries the 4-module white border as well.

Four edges not to cross: do not crop the quiet zone; do not replace white with a transparent background; do not invert the colors, because light modules on a dark background change the light/dark relationship and must be test-scanned on the target device; and do not use gradients, shadows or semi-transparent foregrounds. The tool has no color picker, so these risks live in whatever editing happens after download.

To change size, pick 256/384/512 in the tool again and regenerate; do not stretch a 384px image, which alters the real pixel width of every module and can crop or distort the quiet zone.

VI. Static Codes and Rewritable Short Links: Who Controls the Domain

Once a QR code is printed, its content is fixed; what a scanner reads is usually a URI. RFC 3986 splits a URI into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment: the scheme names the protocol, the host inside the authority says which server to contact, and path and query decide which resource is requested. What happens after the scan depends on the server the URI points to, not on the pattern itself.

A static code writes the final address into the pattern, so a changed address means a reprint. A rewritable short link writes your own domain into the pattern and lets the server send a 3xx redirect to the current target: section 15.4 of RFC 9110 groups 301, 302, 307 and 308 as redirects that indicate a new URI through the Location header, and section 15.4.3 describes 302 Found as the target living temporarily under another URI, with the redirect subject to change.

The price is a transfer of control: whoever holds the short-link domain and the redirect configuration can change the final page, a service going down or a certificate expiring breaks codes already on paper, and a domain changing hands can send scanners to someone else's page. For anything posted long-term, confirm domain ownership, auditable redirects, and a way to export the final addresses if the service ends.

The link itself deserves a second look. The URL parser on this site breaks an address into protocol, hostname, port, path, query and fragment and lists each query parameter; an address carrying user:pass@ shows the user name and password separately, and credentials like that do not belong in a QR code. Section 6.2.2.1 of RFC 3986 also reminds us that scheme and host are case-insensitive, so do not separate a "trusted domain" from an untrusted one by capitalization.

VII. A Pre-Publication Verification List

Verify "it generates" separately from "it scans, and scans to the right place". The list below runs from highest to lowest risk and works as a pass before printing or posting.

Check How to do it If it fails
Content and destination Check protocol, hostname, path and parameters with the URL parser Regenerate; do not hand-edit the image
Capacity and version Confirm the content sits inside the version 40 capacity for the level in use Compare module density first, then raise the level or shorten the content
Size and modules Convert to millimeters per module at the final size Increase the print size; do not stretch the image
Contrast and quiet zone Confirm dark modules, a light background and an unbroken quiet zone on all four sides Export again; do not crop the border or invert the colors
Device and lighting Scan once on at least two devices, under the target lighting and at the target distance Keep a record sample and go back to size and version
Redirect and ownership For a short link, confirm domain ownership, status code and landing page Move to your own domain or to a static code

The item most often skipped is "device and lighting". Zooming in on a monitor and scanning once indoors with the same phone says nothing about a poster, a table card or packaging. Change to a second device, change the distance, scan again in dim light, and when it fails record whether the result was "not detected" or "wrong destination" — the two point at different causes.

VIII. Common Misconceptions

  • "Pick H and everything is fine": H raises recovery at codeword level, but the same content is pushed to a higher version with smaller modules, and capacity drops from 2953 bytes to 1273 bytes.
  • "If it generates, it scans": generating only proves the content fits into some version; module pixels, contrast, quiet zone, printing and lighting all affect recognition.
  • "QR codes expire on their own": the pattern does not age by itself — what breaks is the page it points to, the short-link service, or the credentials.
  • "A barcode works as a URL entry too": barcode mode outputs a one-dimensional CODE128 (bar width 2, bar height 80, quiet zone 12), which suits scanner guns; it has no error-correction level and is a poor carrier for a URL meant to be opened by a phone camera.
  • "Changing settings leaves the generated image alone": editing the content, size or level clears the preview and disables download at once; files already saved do not change, and every edit needs a fresh generate and export.

IX. Boundaries and Limits

The limits are clear: the only types are QR code and barcode (Code128); QR sizes are only 256/384/512 and levels only L/M/Q/H; foreground and background are fixed, with no recoloring, no logo and no quiet-zone tuning; the export file name is always clover-code.png; generation and download both happen locally in the browser, so the tool never visits the target address and does not check whether a link resolves, whether it redirects, or whether a certificate is valid.

Switching to barcode hides the correction field and disables the size dropdown, because CODE128 has no correction level of the kind QR codes use; the barcode is rendered as SVG and still exports as PNG. It suits asset labels and stock barcodes read by a scanner gun, and should not carry a URL meant to be opened by a phone camera.

The tool also does not judge whether the content is safe: a QR code only draws bytes into a pattern, it does not check domain reputation, detect malicious links, or stop you from encoding a Wi-Fi password or a URL carrying credentials. Content review and permission checks belong outside the tool, before publication; the figures in this article come from reproducing qrcode 1.5.4 and the current page implementation, and are not a compatibility promise for any particular printer or scanning app.

faqs.q: Does a higher error-correction level always mean a higher scan success rate?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Level H can recover more codewords, but the same content is pushed to a higher version with denser modules; at an unchanged print size the pixels or millimetres per module actually get smaller. Choose the level from the usage environment first, then verify the final size on the target device.

faqs.q: What can I do when the content is too long and generation fails?
faqs.a: Byte capacity at version 40 is 2953 for L, 2331 for M, 1663 for Q and 1273 for H; beyond that the tool reports "The amount of data is too big to be stored in a QR Code". Shorten the link or move to your own domain rather than forcing the content in by lowering the correction level.

faqs.q: Can a 384px QR code go straight to print?
faqs.a: 384px at 300dpi is about 32.5mm wide; a version 2 module is about 0.99mm and a version 40 module only about 0.18mm. Convert to millimetres per module at the final size before printing, and test-scan on the target device under the target lighting.

faqs.q: How do I choose between a static code and a short-link QR code?
faqs.a: A static code writes the final address into the pattern, so changing the address means a reprint. A short link writes your own domain into the pattern and uses a 3xx redirect to change the destination. The short link is more convenient, but the final destination is decided by whoever controls the domain and the redirect configuration.
